paper_metadata.title: High temperature tensile behaviour of a Cu–1.5 wt.% Ti alloy

evidence.quote: The high temperature tensile properties of a Cu–1.5 wt.% Ti alloy have been investigated in the temperature range of 100–550 °C.

A 30 kg melt of Cu–1.5Ti alloy was vacuum induction melted in a STOKES vacuum induction melting (VIM) furnace at a vacuum of 10−3 torr and cast, after pouring at a temperature of 1200 °C into a graphite mould which was allowed to solidify in vacuum in the mould chamber of the VIM furnace. The ingot was homogenised at 850 °C for 24 h and analyzed for Ti content. The analyzed composition of the ingot was found to be 1.5 wt.% Ti.
The high temperature tensile properties of a Cu–1.5 wt.% Ti alloy have been investigated in the temperature range of 100–550 °C.
The ingot was homogenised at 850 °C for 24 h and analyzed for Ti content. The analyzed composition of the ingot was found to be 1.5 wt.% Ti.
In the peak aged Cu –1.5Ti alloy, the yield as well as tensile strength was found to be nearly independent of temperature up to 350 °C and started decreasing thereafter.

A 30 kg melt of Cu–1.5Ti alloy was vacuum induction melted in a STOKES vacuum induction melting (VIM) furnace at a vacuum of 10−3 torr and cast, after pouring at a temperature of 1200 °C into a graphite mould which was allowed to solidify in vacuum in the mould chamber of the VIM furnace.
The ingot was homogenised at 850 °C for 24 h and analyzed for Ti content.
The homogenised ingot was hot forged and rolled, after soaking at 850 °C for 2 h, into 10 mm thick flats and 12 mm diameter rods.

Round tensile samples with 4.0 mm gauge diameter and 25 mm gauge length were made, solution treated and aged for maximum strength. The details of solution treatment and ageing have been reported elsewhere [15].

The increase in both yield and tensile strengths with increasing temperature up to 450 °C is explained on the basis of in situ age hardening occurring in the solution treated Cu –1.5Ti alloy with the formation of ordered, metastable and coherent Cu4Ti (/p981) precipitate [15,16].
However, beyond 450 °C, the precipitates grow and become coarse, in which case, the dislocations take a path round the precipitate particles, thus the strength decreases.

Both yield and tensile strengths decrease beyond 350 °C due to these coarse precipitate particles as well as thermally activated cross-slip occurring at high temperatures, which would make the movement of the dislocations easy.
